gmat-quant.title: GMAT Quant — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
gmat-quant.summary: Master GMAT Focus Quantitative Reasoning: Problem Solving only, 21 questions in 45 minutes with section-level adaptive difficulty and smart time management.

slides.title: GMAT Focus Edition Overview
points: Three sections: Quant, Verbal, Data Insights (45 min each)
Adaptive at section level — first 5 questions set difficulty range
Score ranges: 60–90 per section, 205–805 total (new scale)
Can bookmark and edit answers to up to 3 questions per section
No calculator in Quant; calculator in Data Insights

example.label: Adaptive Flow
example.text: Easy Q1→Q2→Q3 = slightly easier Q4–5. Hard Q1→Q2→Q3 = slightly harder Q4–5.

slides.tip: Use the bookmark feature strategically on time-consuming problems; return if you finish early.
slides.warn: You cannot skip sections or return to previous sections once done.

slides.title: Quant Timing & Format
points: 21 questions in 45 minutes (~2 min 8 sec per question)
Problem Solving ONLY — Data Sufficiency removed in Focus Edition
Questions get harder/easier based on accuracy (adaptive)
No scratch paper allowed; use on-screen tools for work
Multiple choice: 5 answer choices per question
slides.tip: Speed comes from pattern recognition, not rushed calculation. Slow down on setup.
slides.warn: Do NOT aim for 100% accuracy; targeting 80–85% correct with smart time saves you.

slides.title: Problem Solving Strategies
points: Read the question twice; identify what's being asked
Ballpark before diving into algebra or long calculations
Use answer choices to guide approach (plug-in, backsolve)
Number line / coordinate system sketches save time
Avoid calculator dependency — estimate when possible

example.label: Plug & Check
example.text: If Q asks 'which value of x?' — plug each answer choice into the problem, starting with C or middle value.

slides.tip: Estimate first. If 5 answer choices cluster, use that to narrow before calculating exactly.
slides.warn: Careless algebra mistakes (sign errors, distribution) account for ~30% of wrong answers.

slides.title: Arithmetic & Number Properties
points: Integers, primes, divisibility, remainders, factors, multiples
Fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios, rates
Powers, roots, exponents, scientific notation
Absolute value, odd/even, positive/negative
GCD, LCM, number bases

example.label: Remainders
example.text: If 47 ÷ 5 = 9 remainder 2, then 47 = 5(9) + 2. Use remainders to solve 'what number leaves remainder 3 when divided by 7?'

slides.tip: Memorize: squares up to 20, primes up to 50, key fractions (1/6, 1/8, etc.).
slides.warn: Percent problems: 'increase by 20%' ≠ 'is 20% more.' Read modifiers carefully.

slides.title: Algebra Fundamentals
points: Linear equations, systems of equations, inequalities
Quadratic equations: factoring, completing the square, quadratic formula
Polynomials, exponent rules, radicals
Functions, domain and range, substitution
Graphing lines and parabolas

example.label: Quadratic
example.text: Solve 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0. Factor as (2x − 1)(x + 3) = 0, so x = 1/2 or x = −3.

slides.tip: If a quadratic doesn't factor easily, use the quadratic formula; don't waste time guessing.
slides.warn: When solving inequalities, FLIP the sign if multiplying/dividing by a negative number.

slides.title: Word Problems: Setup & Translation
points: Identify unknowns and define variables clearly
Translate English to math: 'sum' = +, 'product' = ×, 'percent of' = multiply
Set up equation step-by-step; don't jump to the answer
Check units (hours, dollars, people) match throughout
Plug your answer back into the original problem

example.label: Work Rate
example.text: If Alice does 1/3 of a job per hour and Bob does 1/5 per hour, together they do 1/3 + 1/5 = 8/15 per hour.

slides.tip: For rate problems, use: rate × time = work. For mixture, track each component separately.
slides.warn: Read carefully: 'three times as many' ≠ 'three more than.' These flip the equation.

slides.title: Distance, Rate & Time Problems
points: Distance = Rate × Time. Rearrange for rate or time as needed.
Average speed ≠ average of speeds. Use total distance / total time.
Relative speed: approaching = sum of speeds, same direction = difference
Use a table for multi-leg journeys (leg 1: d, r, t; leg 2: d, r, t; total: Σd, avg r, Σt)
Watch units: convert hours/minutes, miles/km consistently

example.label: Average Speed
example.text: Drive 120 miles at 60 mph, then 120 miles at 40 mph. Average speed = 240 / (2 + 3) = 48 mph, not 50 mph.

slides.tip: If told 'A leaves at 8 AM, B leaves at 9 AM,' track the head start explicitly in your table.
slides.warn: Do NOT average speeds by adding and dividing by 2 unless distances are equal.

slides.title: Percentage & Profit/Loss Problems
points: Percent = (part / whole) × 100. Watch direction: 'X is what percent of Y?'
Percent increase = (new − old) / old × 100
Compound growth: Final = Initial × (1 + rate)^n
Profit = Revenue − Cost. Profit margin = (Profit / Cost) × 100
Successive percents multiply: 10% increase then 10% decrease ≠ back to original

example.label: Compound
example.text: Invest $1000 at 5% annual interest for 2 years: Final = 1000 × (1.05)² = $1102.50.

slides.tip: For successive discounts, multiply multipliers: 20% off then 10% off = 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72 (28% off total).
slides.warn: Interest: simple vs compound matters. Simple = P + (P × r × t). Compound = P(1 + r)^t.

slides.title: Combination & Permutation Basics
points: Permutation (order matters): n! / (n−r)! or nPr. Example: arrange 3 books from 5 = 5×4×3.
Combination (order doesn't): n! / (r!(n−r)!) or nCr. Example: choose 3 books from 5 = 10.
Probability = favorable outcomes / total outcomes
Independent events: P(A AND B) = P(A) × P(B)

example.label: Combination
example.text: Choose 2 people from 4 for a committee: C(4,2) = 4! / (2! × 2!) = 6 ways.

slides.tip: Ask: does order matter? If yes, permutation. If no, combination.
slides.warn: Probability ≠ odds. P(event) = 1/3 means odds are 1:2 (not 1:3).

slides.title: Geometry: Angles, Triangles & Polygons
points: Angle sum in triangle = 180°. In n-gon = (n−2) × 180°.
Right triangle: Pythagorean theorem a² + b² = c². Special triangles: 45-45-90, 30-60-90.
Triangle inequality: sum of any two sides > third side
Congruent triangles: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL
Similar triangles: angles equal, sides proportional. Ratio of areas = (ratio of sides)²

example.label: Special Right Triangle
example.text: In 45-45-90: if leg = 5, hypotenuse = 5√2. In 30-60-90: if short leg = 3, long leg = 3√3, hypotenuse = 6.

slides.tip: Sketch triangles. Label angles and sides. Use Pythagorean theorem even if you don't see a right angle yet.
slides.warn: Similar ≠ congruent. Similar triangles have same shape, different size.

slides.title: Circles, Area & Perimeter
points: Circle: circumference = 2πr, area = πr². Radius, diameter, chord, arc, sector.
Arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr (θ in degrees) or θ × r (θ in radians)
Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr²
Inscribed angle = 1/2 central angle
Tangent line perpendicular to radius at point of tangency

example.label: Sector
example.text: Circle with radius 6, sector angle 60°. Sector area = (60/360) × π(6)² = 6π.

slides.tip: Memorize π ≈ 3.14 or 22/7 for quick estimation in multiple-choice.
slides.warn: Don't confuse arc length with arc area. Arc length is a distance; sector area is area.

slides.title: 3D Geometry: Volume & Surface Area
points: Rectangular solid: V = l × w × h, surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh)
Cylinder: V = πr²h, lateral area = 2πrh, total surface = 2πr² + 2πrh
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, surface area = 4πr²
Cone: V = (1/3)πr²h, lateral area = πrl (l = slant height)
Diagonal of rectangular solid = √(l² + w² + h²)

example.label: Cylinder
example.text: Cylinder with r = 3, h = 10. Volume = π(3)²(10) = 90π. Surface area = 2π(3)² + 2π(3)(10) = 78π.

slides.tip: For tricky shapes, break into simpler solids and add/subtract volumes.
slides.warn: Slant height ≠ height. Slant height is on the surface; height is perpendicular to base.

slides.title: Coordinate Geometry & Distance
points: Distance formula: d = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]
Midpoint: M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)
Slope: m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁). Parallel slopes equal. Perpendicular slopes = negative reciprocal.
Line equation: y = mx + b (slope-intercept), or Ax + By = C (standard)
Reflection, rotation, translation preserve distance and angles
slides.tip: Sketch on graph paper. Visual check often catches errors faster than algebra.
slides.warn: Slope of vertical line is undefined (not infinity). Slope of horizontal line is 0.

slides.title: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mode & Range
points: Mean (average) = sum / count
Median = middle value when ordered (average of two middle if even count)
Mode = most frequent value. No mode if all values appear once.
Range = max − min
Standard deviation measures spread. Higher SD = wider spread.
slides.tip: If mean > median, data is skewed right (outliers pull mean up). Left skew = mean < median.
slides.warn: Median is less affected by outliers than mean. Use median for skewed distributions.

slides.title: Probability & Expected Value
points: Probability P(event) ∈ [0, 1]. Sum of all outcomes = 1.
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) [inclusion-exclusion]
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A) [conditional]. For independent: P(A) × P(B).
Expected value E(X) = Σ(outcome × probability)
Standard deviation σ = √(variance)

example.label: Independent Events
example.text: Flip coin (1/2 heads), roll die (1/6 six). P(heads AND six) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.

slides.tip: For 'at least one' problems, use complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
slides.warn: Conditional probability P(A|B) ≠ P(A). Include the given condition in your sample space.

slides.title: Sequences & Series (Arithmetic & Geometric)
points: Arithmetic sequence: each term = previous + common difference d. nth term = a + (n−1)d.
Arithmetic sum: S_n = n/2 × (first + last)
Geometric sequence: each term = previous × common ratio r. nth term = a × r^(n−1).
Geometric sum (finite): S_n = a(1 − r^n) / (1 − r)
Geometric sum (infinite, |r| < 1): S = a / (1 − r)
slides.tip: Identify the pattern first: constant difference = arithmetic; constant ratio = geometric.
slides.warn: For infinite geometric series, convergence requires |r| < 1. If |r| ≥ 1, sum diverges.

slides.title: Exponents & Radicals Rules
points: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n). a^m / a^n = a^(m−n). (a^m)^n = a^(mn).
a^(−n) = 1/a^n. a^(1/n) = nth root of a.
Rationalize: 1/√2 = √2/2. (1/(a+√b)) × (a−√b)/(a−√b) to eliminate radicals.
Note: √a² = |a| (not always a). For positive a: √a² = a.
slides.tip: Convert radicals to fractional exponents for easier algebra: ∛(x²) = x^(2/3).
slides.warn: √(a² + b²) ≠ a + b. Do NOT split radicals across addition/subtraction.

slides.title: Common Trap: Algebra Pitfalls
points: Distributing wrong: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6, not 2x + 3.
Crossing products in proportion: if a/b = c/d, then ad = bc (not ac = bd).
Squaring both sides introduces extraneous solutions. Always check.
Dividing by a variable or expression may exclude solutions. Be careful with zero.
Absolute value: |x| = 5 means x = 5 OR x = −5. Don't forget the negative case.

example.label: Extraneous Solutions
example.text: Solve √(x+2) = x. Square both sides: x+2 = x². Rearrange: x² − x − 2 = 0. Solutions: x = 2 or x = −1. Check: √(2+2) = 2 ✓; √(−1+2) = −1 ✗. Answer: x = 2 only.

slides.tip: Always substitute your final answer back into the original equation to verify.
slides.warn: Negative numbers under even roots are undefined (in real numbers). Watch domain restrictions.

slides.title: Test Strategy: Pacing & Bookmarks
points: Scan all 21 questions first (30 sec). Mark any looking 'tricky' to return to.
Do confident, faster questions first. Build momentum and time bank.
Use 2-3 bookmarks on genuinely difficult or time-heavy problems.
If stuck after 1 min 30 sec, bookmark, guess, move on. Return if time allows.
Last 5 min: quick review of bookmarked Qs. Don't change correct answers.

example.label: Example Pacing
example.text: Q1–5 (easy, ~1:30 each): 7:30 elapsed. Q6–10 (medium, ~2 min): 17:30 elapsed. Q11–21 (hard, ~2:30): 42:30 elapsed.

slides.tip: Spend less time on early questions, more on later ones (they're worth more in adaptive scoring).
slides.warn: Rushing early questions for speed is a trap. Get them right; time comes naturally from confidence.

slides.title: Top Mistakes in Quant
points: Careless arithmetic: typos in long calculations. Double-check multiplications.
Misreading: 'of' = multiply; 'is' = equals. Read modifiers (percent, ratio, rate).
Wrong approach: spending 3+ min on one problem when backsolving would take 30 sec.
Forgetting to check both positive and negative solutions (e.g., √x = 3 → x = 9, not −9).
Using calculator mindlessly. Estimate first; calculator is for verification.

example.label: Misreading Trap
example.text: Q: '3 times as many apples as oranges.' If o = oranges, then a = 3o (not a = o + 3).

slides.tip: On Practice tests, log your mistakes (arithmetic vs strategy vs misread). Fix patterns.
slides.warn: The hardest GMAT Quant problems test logic and setup, not calculator skill.

slides.title: Data Sufficiency Removal: What Changed
points: GMAT Focus removed Data Sufficiency from Quant entirely.
All 21 Quant questions are now Problem Solving only.
This means 25% more word problems, rates, geometry, and algebra—not 'is this info enough' logic.
Freed-up brain space: focus on solving, not analyzing two statements.
Old GMAT prep books still mix DS questions—filter for Focus Edition only.

example.label: Old vs New
example.text: Old GMAT Quant: 11 PS + 10 DS. New GMAT Focus Quant: 21 PS, 0 DS.

slides.tip: If you studied Data Sufficiency, unlearning it takes mental discipline. Redirect that energy to problem-solving depth.
slides.warn: Do NOT use old Data Sufficiency questions for practice. They don't reflect the current test.

slides.title: Advanced Technique: Backsolving
points: Plug answer choices into the problem instead of solving algebraically.
Start with middle choice (C) if answer choices are ordered numerically.
If C is too big, try A or B next. If too small, try D or E.
Saves setup time and algebra errors on complicated word problems.
Only works for 'find the value' questions, not 'which statement' type.

example.label: Backsolve Example
example.text: Q: 'If x is an integer and 2x + 5 = 13, find x.' Try C (x = 4): 2(4) + 5 = 13 ✓. Answer: x = 4.

slides.tip: Backsolving is faster on time-pressure questions. Master it for test day.
slides.warn: Not all problems have 'nice' numeric answer choices. Backsolving fails on 'which expression' answers.

slides.title: Advanced Technique: Number Picking
points: Replace variables with concrete numbers (small, positive integers or 0/1).
Plug into the question and answer choices to eliminate wrong answers.
Especially useful for ratio, percent, and algebra problems.
Avoid 0, 1, negative, or fractions on first pick unless specifically needed.
Check multiple numbers if several answers seem right.

example.label: Pick Numbers
example.text: Q: 'If x is 20% of y, then y is what percent of x?' Pick y = 10, so x = 2. Then x/y = 2/10 = 20%. Answer is 'x is 20% of y.'

slides.tip: Number picking works best when the problem has 'variables in the answers' (all choices have x, y, or %).
slides.warn: Always verify your picked numbers satisfy the original condition. Don't introduce extraneous solutions.

slides.title: Building Problem Intuition
points: Solve 50+ problems of each type (rates, geometry, sequences, etc.) with a target.
Time each: track how fast you solve correctly vs how long you waste on traps.
After each problem, read the official explanation—learn the 'cleaner' method.
Group similar problems and find the underlying pattern (e.g., 'all use Pythagorean theorem').
Review wrong answers in a notebook: what triggered the mistake? (arithmetic, logic, misread?)

example.label: Pattern Recognition
example.text: After 10 work-rate problems, you notice: always use 1/(rate) for time per job, then sum rates. Pattern = leverage.

slides.tip: Volume beats speed. Solve many; do not overthink 1–2 hard problems.
slides.warn: Studying explanations is NOT the same as solving. Always solve first, then read why your approach was wrong.

slides.title: Practice Resources & Next Steps
points: Official GMAC tests (GMATPrep) have real, adaptive questions—use these for full-length mocks.
Syllab's free GMAT mocks (gmat section drills) build timing and adaptive feedback.
Khan Academy covers fundamentals; GMAT Club forums have solved problems.
Target 80–85% accuracy on Quant (not 100%) to manage time well.
Simulate test conditions: 45 min, timed, no pausing, pen & paper for scrap work.

example.label: Practice Plan
example.text: Weeks 1–4: drill by topic (algebra, geometry, rates 50 Qs each). Weeks 5–7: full-section tests. Week 8: review errors, resimulate.

slides.tip: Take a full GMAT Focus mock after 3 weeks to establish baseline; use results to prioritize weak areas.
slides.warn: Avoid 'analysis paralysis'—practice > review for most test-takers. Solve, review errors, move on.

slides.title: Final Checklist: Day Before the Test
points: Review your error log (top 5 patterns: careless math, misreading, wrong approach).
Do ONE full 45-min timed Quant section (not a full 3-section mock).
Verify you know formulas (circle, Pythagorean, rate = distance/time, etc.).
Sleep well. No cramming new topics the day before.
On test day: warm up with 3–4 easy problems. Build confidence before hard ones start adapting.

example.label: Warm-Up Routine
example.text: Test day, before Quant starts: do 2 mental arithmetic Qs (no calculator), 1 basic algebra. Sharpen mindset.

slides.tip: Confidence and calm matter more than last-minute cramming. Trust your 4–6 weeks of prep.
slides.warn: Do NOT try new techniques on test day. Stick to methods you drilled.

slides.title: Closing: Your Quant Win
points: GMAT Focus Quant is 21 Problem Solving questions, 45 minutes, no Data Sufficiency.
Success = accuracy (80–85%) + pacing (2–3 min/Q average) + calm under pressure.
Master the topic fundamentals first; then learn tricks and shortcuts.
Use the 3-bookmark feature to flag time-heavy or uncertain problems.
Practice with realistic mocks to build adaptive instinct.

example.label: Your Target
example.text: Score goal: Q80–90 (75th+ percentile). Strategy: 80% accuracy, strong fundamentals, calm pacing.

slides.tip: Every Q you solve correctly increases your odds of seeing harder, higher-scoring questions next.
slides.warn: There is no 'trick' to GMAT Quant—only solid fundamentals, practice, and discipline. Embrace it.

gmat-verbal.title: GMAT Verbal — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
gmat-verbal.summary: Master GMAT Focus Verbal: Critical Reasoning and Reading Comprehension only, 23 questions in 45 minutes with section-level adaptive pacing and real passage analysis.

slides.title: Verbal Section Overview (GMAT Focus Edition)
points: 23 questions in 45 minutes (~1 min 57 sec per question)
Two question types ONLY: Critical Reasoning (CR) and Reading Comprehension (RC)
NO Sentence Correction in Focus Edition (grammar-only questions removed)
Section-level adaptive: first 5 Qs set difficulty band for remaining 18
Can bookmark up to 3 questions and edit answers during the section

example.label: Composition
example.text: Typical mix: 10–11 CR questions + 12–13 RC questions. Passages are long (400–600 words) and require careful reading.

slides.tip: Since no grammar rules are tested in Focus, you must focus on argument logic and comprehension, not syntax.
slides.warn: Old prep materials with Sentence Correction are NOT applicable to GMAT Focus. Ignore them.

slides.title: Verbal Timing & Pacing Strategy
points: CR questions: ~1:30–1:45 per question (shorter passages, quicker)
RC questions: ~2:30–3:00 per question (long passages, slower)
Read the question first, then the passage, to know what to hunt for
Do easy questions first to build confidence and time bank
Flag 2–3 genuinely tough Qs; return if time remains (last 2–3 min)

example.label: Time Budget
example.text: 10 CR @ 1:45 = 17:30. 13 RC @ 2:45 = 35:45. 9:15 min buffer for review.

slides.tip: Easier CR questions often appear first; harder RC passages come later. Expect the difficulty ramp.
slides.warn: Do NOT spend 3+ min on a single RC question. Guess, flag, return after finishing the passage.

slides.title: Critical Reasoning: Argument Anatomy
points: Every CR question has: premise (evidence) + conclusion (claim) + sometimes assumption
Identify what the author claims and why they claim it
Assumptions are UNSTATED beliefs the argument relies on
Logical flaws: circular reasoning, false cause, false analogy, overgeneralization
Question type tells you what to assess: strengthen, weaken, assumption, inference, paradox

example.label: Argument Breakdown
example.text: P: 'Vitamin D improves bone health.' P: 'Study X shows people taking Vitamin D have stronger bones.' C: 'Everyone should take Vitamin D.' (Assumption: the study is representative of all populations.)

slides.tip: Mark the premises with 'P' and conclusion with 'C' in your scratch work. It clarifies the argument.
slides.warn: Conclusion often appears at the START of the argument, not at the end. Read for signal words: 'thus,' 'so,' 'therefore.'

slides.title: Critical Reasoning: Strengthen the Argument
points: Find the assumption first. Then ask: which answer supports that assumption?
Strengthen = add evidence that makes the conclusion more likely
New evidence that bridges the gap between premise and conclusion is strongest
Avoid answers that 'seem related' but don't logically support the claim
Eliminate answers that weaken, contradict, or are irrelevant

example.label: Strengthen
example.text: Argument: 'Coffee drinkers live longer, so coffee extends lifespan.' Assumption: correlation = causation. Strengthen: 'Studies controlling for diet and exercise still show coffee drinkers live 3 years longer.'

slides.tip: Strongest answers remove a reasonable objection to the argument. What would a skeptic say?
slides.warn: Answers that 'support the topic' are not the same as 'strengthen the argument.' Stay focused on the logic chain.

slides.title: Critical Reasoning: Weaken the Argument
points: Weaken = introduce doubt about the conclusion
Attack the assumption, not the premise. Premises are given; you can't disprove them.
Alternative explanation: show the conclusion could be false even if premises are true
Eliminate the necessity of the conclusion: show the evidence could lead elsewhere
Avoid extreme weakeners; subtle logical undermining is often correct

example.label: Weaken
example.text: Argument: 'Ice cream sales increase in summer, so warmer weather causes people to eat ice cream.' Weaken: 'Ice cream sales also spike around holidays, when weather is cold.' (Alternative cause: holidays, not heat.)

slides.tip: The best weaken answers point out a logical gap the author overlooked, not a minor factual error.
slides.warn: Do NOT confuse 'weaken' with 'support an opposite conclusion.' You're questioning the current logic, not proving the opposite.

slides.title: Critical Reasoning: Assumption & Inference
points: Assumption: unstated belief required for the argument to work. Ask: 'What MUST be true?'
Inference (conclusion): what logically follows from the premises. Ask: 'What CAN you conclude?'
Assumption answers are often negations: 'The author assumes X is NOT the case.'
Inference is weaker than logical proof; it's based on the passage, not external knowledge
For inference, choose the most supported answer, not the most extreme conclusion

example.label: Assumption vs Inference
example.text: Premise: 'All birds lay eggs.' Premise: 'Penguins are birds.' Assumption: 'Eggs are the typical bird offspring.' Inference: 'Penguins lay eggs.'

slides.tip: Negation test for assumptions: if you negate the answer and the argument falls apart, it's the assumption.
slides.warn: Inferences must be supported by the passage. Don't bring outside knowledge or 'common sense.'

slides.title: Critical Reasoning: Paradox & Explain the Discrepancy
points: Paradox question: two facts seem to contradict. Find the answer that resolves it.
The resolution must explain how BOTH facts can be true simultaneously
Look for hidden scope: 'coffee extends lifespan' (for whom? which group?) vs 'coffee shortens lifespan' (for different group)
Time-based resolutions: 'coffee helps short-term, hurts long-term' reconciles opposite findings
Avoid answers that simply restate the facts. You need a bridging explanation.

example.label: Paradox
example.text: Fact 1: 'Smartphones increase teen anxiety.' Fact 2: 'Teens with smartphones report better social connections.' Resolution: 'Smartphones improve online social bonds but reduce face-to-face interactions, increasing overall anxiety.'

slides.tip: Paradox resolutions often exploit scope differences (adults vs teens, short-term vs long-term, online vs offline).
slides.warn: The 'explain the discrepancy' answer doesn't need to be what's actually true—just logically possible given the facts.

slides.title: Critical Reasoning: Logical Fallacies to Know
points: Ad hominem: attacks the person, not the argument ('You're biased, so your claim is false.')
Circular reasoning: conclusion is the same as a premise ('X is true because X is true.')
False cause: 'A happened before B, so A caused B.' (Post hoc ergo propter hoc)
False analogy: two things seem similar but differ in a crucial way
Overgeneralization: 'Some Xs have property Y, therefore all Xs have Y.'

example.label: Fallacy
example.text: Argument: 'My neighbor smoked and got cancer, so smoking causes cancer in my neighborhood.' Fallacy: anecdote ≠ evidence, overgeneralization.

slides.tip: Recognize fallacies during the first read. They are often the basis of weaken or flaw questions.
slides.warn: Not every logical jump is a 'fallacy.' The GMAT tests common, teachable flaws, not esoteric logical errors.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension: First Read Strategy
points: Preview the questions first (10–15 sec) to know the passage's 'hot spots' (main idea, author tone, specific details)
Read the passage ONCE, without stopping to re-read. Pace: 2.5–3 min per passage.
Mark main idea in paragraph 1 and any shifts in logic (but, however, on the other hand)
Note tone (critical, neutral, supportive) and author's purpose (explain, argue, defend, critique)
Do not highlight excessively. Annotation is a guide, not a study tool.

example.label: Preview & Read
example.text: Questions mention 'author's view on X' and 'details about Y.' Read looking for these. Mark ¶ where X and Y appear.

slides.tip: GMAT RC passages are dense but purposeful. Every sentence serves a function. Understand the structure.
slides.warn: Do NOT re-read the passage for every question. Use your margin notes and move on.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension: Main Idea & Tone
points: Main idea ≠ topic. Topic is the subject (e.g., 'photosynthesis'). Main idea is the author's point about it.
Tone reflects the author's attitude: critical, appreciative, neutral, skeptical, etc.
Scope: narrow ('the history of X in region Y') vs broad ('X across all regions')
Purpose: explain a phenomenon, defend a position, critique a theory, reconcile a contradiction
Wrong main-idea answers overstate, understate, or reverse the author's actual point

example.label: Main Idea
example.text: Topic: 'Artificial Intelligence.' Main idea: 'AI is transforming healthcare diagnostics, though privacy concerns remain unresolved.' Tone: optimistic but cautious.

slides.tip: Main idea is the 'takeaway' after finishing the passage. It should fit in one sentence.
slides.warn: Avoid extremes like 'completely revolutionized' or 'utterly failed' if the passage is measured and balanced.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension: Inference & Evidence
points: Inference: what follows logically from the passage, even if not explicitly stated
Look for signal words: 'suggests,' 'implies,' 'indicates,' 'most likely'
Wrong inference answers require outside knowledge or contradict the passage
Textual evidence: every correct answer has support within 5–10 lines of the passage
For 'according to the passage,' answer must match the text exactly (not close, exact)

example.label: Inference
example.text: Passage: 'The company reported a 30% decline in Q4 revenue but maintains aggressive expansion plans.' Inference: 'The company is optimistic despite recent losses' (supported by 'maintains expansion') vs 'The company failed' (too extreme).

slides.tip: For inference, choose the most conservative answer supported by the text. Avoid leaps.
slides.warn: Inference ≠ assumption. Inference is what the passage implies; assumption is what the author takes for granted.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension: Detail Questions
points: Detail questions ask for specific facts: numbers, names, sequence, definition
Correct answers are usually reworded, not copied from the passage (watch for synonyms)
Wrong details often invert the truth: 'increased' becomes 'decreased' or 'true' becomes 'false'
Use line numbers from questions to locate the relevant section (usually 5–15 lines)
If unsure, re-read that section carefully and eliminate half-truths

example.label: Detail Question
example.text: Q: 'The 18th-century movement emphasized individual liberty.' Correct reword: 'The 18th-century era valued personal autonomy.' Wrong: 'The 18th century invented the concept of freedom' (too broad).

slides.tip: Detail questions are often faster than inference. Use them to build momentum.
slides.warn: Rewordings can be subtle. 'Some experts' ≠ 'all experts.' 'May' ≠ 'will.' Read carefully.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension: Author's Opinion vs Fact
points: Distinguish factual statements (neutral) from author's commentary (opinionated)
Author's opinion appears in thesis, topic sentences, conclusions, and signal phrases: 'I believe,' 'unfortunately,' 'notably'
If a passage says 'some argue X' but 'the author contends Y,' those are different
Questions like 'the author would agree' require identifying the author's stance, not just the topic
Tone and opinion are closely linked. Negative tone = critical opinion.

example.label: Opinion vs Fact
example.text: Fact: 'The climate has warmed 1.1°C since 1850.' Opinion: 'This alarming trend demands immediate action.' (Author opinion = action is needed.)

slides.tip: Highlight topic sentences and the conclusion. The author's opinion is concentrated there.
slides.warn: Quoted or paraphrased opinions (e.g., 'Critics claim...') are NOT automatically the author's view. Determine if the author endorses them.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension: Structure & Organization
points: Passages follow patterns: Problem-Solution, Compare-Contrast, Chronology, Definition-Example, Argument-Counterargument
Structural transitions: 'However,' 'yet,' 'despite' signal a contrast or pivot
Identifying structure helps answer 'why did the author include this paragraph?' questions
Questions about paragraph function: 'provide evidence,' 'introduce a counterargument,' 'offer an alternative'
Poor structure: jumping between unrelated ideas, unclear cause-and-effect

example.label: Structure
example.text: ¶1: Problem (healthcare costs rising). ¶2: Current solution (insurance reform). ¶3: Counterargument (critics say insurance alone won't work). ¶4: Author's position (both are needed). Pattern: Argument + Counterargument + Resolution.

slides.tip: Mapping the structure (e.g., P-S-C-R) takes 30 sec and helps answer 5+ questions.
slides.warn: Structure is often tested; don't overlook 'why is paragraph 3 included' type questions.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension: Traps & Distractors
points: Adjacent plausible answers: two seem right, but only one matches the specific question
Out-of-scope: correct fact, but doesn't answer the question asked
Reversed logic: answer is the opposite of the passage
Overgeneralization: passage says 'some'; answer says 'all'
Emotional language: answer uses extreme words ('obviously,' 'utterly') not in the passage

example.label: Trap
example.text: Q: 'Why did the author mention the 1920s?' Trap A: Correct fact from the 1920s section, but not the REASON it was mentioned. Correct B: Explains how the 1920s reference supports the main argument.

slides.tip: When multiple answers seem right, reread the question. It's usually more specific than you first noticed.
slides.warn: The GMAT rewards close reading. One word difference can flip an answer from wrong to right.

slides.title: Verbal Strategy: Picking Your Battles
points: Not all questions are worth the same effort. Some RC passages are harder to parse.
Read question types and estimate effort: 'main idea' is faster than 'infer the author's opinion.'
If a passage is dense, consider flagging its toughest question and returning if time allows
Accuracy > speed. A wrong answer costs more than a guessed answer.
For CR, time-consuming 'explain the paradox' questions can be worth skipping on first pass

example.label: Effort Estimate
example.text: Passage on 18th-century philosophy (dense, technical): Q1 main idea (1 min), Q2 detail (45 sec), Q3 inference (2 min)—SKIP Q3 if time is short.

slides.tip: Mark a question as 'return later' if you've spent 90 sec and aren't confident. Move on.
slides.warn: Skipping too many Qs hurts guessing. Aim for ~1 skip per 45-min section, not more.

slides.title: Sentence Correction Removal: What Changed
points: GMAT Focus removed Sentence Correction from Verbal entirely.
Grammar rules (subject-verb agreement, modifiers, tense) are NO LONGER tested.
Verbal now focuses purely on argument analysis (CR) and reading comprehension (RC).
Old GMAT prep books mix Sentence Correction questions—filter for Focus Edition only.
This shift benefits non-native English speakers (one fewer grammar-heavy section).

example.label: Old vs New
example.text: Old GMAT Verbal: ~6 SC + ~12 CR + ~12 RC. New GMAT Focus Verbal: 0 SC + 10–11 CR + 12–13 RC.

slides.tip: If you studied grammar extensively, good news: you don't need it anymore. Focus on logic and comprehension.
slides.warn: Do NOT use old Sentence Correction materials. They test rules not in GMAT Focus.

slides.title: Building Vocabulary for GMAT Verbal
points: GMAT Verbal uses sophisticated but learnable vocabulary: 'ameliorate,' 'mitigate,' 'erudite,' 'specious'
Vocabulary matters most in CR (arguments use precise words) and some RC passages
Learn word roots, prefixes, suffixes to infer meaning (e.g., 'mis-' = wrong, 'mal-' = bad, 'bene-' = good)
Context clues in passages help you infer meaning even if you don't know the exact word
Practice: flashcards (Anki), etymology lists, reading dense articles (The Economist, journal articles)

example.label: Root Dissection
example.text: 'Counterargument' = against + statement. 'Mitigating circumstances' = lessening factors. Roots unlock meaning.

slides.tip: Learn 50–100 'high-probability GMAT words.' Frequency lists are available free online.
slides.warn: Memorizing a dictionary is inefficient. Focus on words that appear in GMAT prep materials, not random vocab.

slides.title: Critical Reasoning: Argument Types & Patterns
points: Causal argument: 'X caused Y.' Assumption: no other cause explains Y.
Statistical argument: 'Study shows X.' Assumption: study is representative and methodology is sound.
Analogy argument: 'A is like B, so A will do what B does.' Assumption: A and B are similar in the relevant way.
Authority argument: 'Expert says X, so X is true.' Assumption: the expert is credible.
Definitional argument: 'X meets the definition of Y, so X is Y.' Assumption: the definition is correct.

example.label: Causal
example.text: Argument: 'Sales increased after we launched ads, so ads drove sales.' Assumption: no other factor (seasonal, competitor exit, economic shift) explains the increase.

slides.tip: Identifying the argument type helps you spot the assumption and what kind of evidence would weaken it.
slides.warn: Correlation ≠ causation. Many GMAT arguments confuse these. Weaken answers exploit this confusion.

slides.title: Verbal Practice: Build Accuracy Systematically
points: Accuracy > speed. Aim for 75–80% on practice before targeting speed.
Do 20–30 CR questions by type: strengthen, weaken, assumption, inference, paradox.
Read 3–4 RC passages per week. Vary difficulty and subject (science, history, social science).
Time yourself only after mastering accuracy. Then optimize pacing.
Log errors: missed inference, misread a detail, overlooked scope. Fix patterns, not one-offs.

example.label: Practice Schedule
example.text: Week 1: 30 CR (10 strengthen, 10 weaken, 10 assumption). Week 2: 4 RC passages + 20 CR mixed. Week 3: full-section timed (23 Qs, 45 min).

slides.tip: Review explanations even for correct answers. They reveal faster solution paths.
slides.warn: Memorizing arguments or passages doesn't improve skill. Practice diverse passages to build intuition.

slides.title: Advanced: Cross-Passage Comparison (Dual RC)
points: Some RC sections include a paired-passage format: two shorter passages on related topics
Compare structure, tone, and argument between the two passages
Questions ask: 'How do the authors differ?' 'Which passage supports X?'
Strategy: read both passages first (no interleaving), then answer all questions together
Comparison questions often require inference about how authors would react to each other's ideas

example.label: Comparison
example.text: Passage 1: AI is beneficial. Passage 2: AI poses privacy risks. Q: 'How would Author 2 respond to Author 1's argument?' Answer: 'Author 2 would note that benefits don't address privacy.' (Inference from Passage 2's concern.)

slides.tip: Skim both passages to find the key disagreement first. Then answer comparison Qs.
slides.warn: Do NOT confuse Passage 1's view with Passage 2's. Mark 'A1 says X' and 'A2 says Y' to avoid mix-ups.

slides.title: Final Checklist: Verbal Mastery
points: CR: identify premise, conclusion, assumption. Weaken = attack assumption or find alternative cause.
RC: preview questions, read once for structure and tone, use margin notes, don't re-read unless lost.
Pacing: 1:45 per CR, 2:45 per RC Qs. Flag 2–3 toughest; return if time allows.
Vocabulary: learn 50–100 'high-prob GMAT words' and root patterns.
Accuracy target: 80% on practice before optimizing speed.

example.label: Your Score Target
example.text: Verbal goal: V40–45 (75th+ percentile). Strategy: 80% accuracy, strategic skipping, confident fundamentals.

slides.tip: Verbal rewards careful reading and logical thinking more than any 'trick.' Invest in understanding.
slides.warn: Rushing Verbal questions is the #1 mistake. Read completely, analyze fully, answer confidently.

slides.title: Practice Resources & Next Steps
points: Official GMAC tests (GMATPrep) have real, adaptive Verbal sections—essential for pacing.
Syllab's free GMAT mocks provide Verbal-specific drills and adaptive feedback.
GMAT Club forums have solved CR and RC explanations for deeper understanding.
Read challenging articles (The Economist, science journals) to build comprehension speed.
Take one full 45-min Verbal section every week to simulate test conditions.

example.label: Weekly Practice
example.text: Mon/Wed: 20 CR by type + 15 min reading (article). Tue/Thu: 2 RC passages + 15 CR mixed. Sat: full-section mock.

slides.tip: Engage with passages actively. Ask, 'Why did the author write this?' for every main idea question.
slides.warn: Passive reading (highlighting without thinking) doesn't build inference skills. Annotate purposefully.

slides.title: Verbal Test Day: Confidence & Execution
points: Warm-up: read 2 short articles (5 min) to get into 'reading mode' before the test.
Mental reset between questions: breathe, clear your head, focus on the next Q.
Do NOT second-guess correct answers. If you're confident, move on.
Flag tough Qs but don't dwell. Guess and move on if you're past 2 min.
Last 2–3 min: quick gut check on flagged Qs. Change only if you spot a clear error.

example.label: Test Day Flow
example.text: Read 1 article (3 min). Sit for Verbal. Q1–5 (build momentum). Q6–23 (pace, flag as needed). Last 2 min: review flags.

slides.tip: Confidence comes from practice, not luck. By test day, you've solved 100+ CR and RC Qs. Trust it.
slides.warn: Anxiety is normal. Expect hard passages and tricky questions. They're testing everyone equally.

slides.title: Closing: Your Verbal Win
points: GMAT Focus Verbal is 23 questions (10–11 CR + 12–13 RC), 45 minutes, no grammar.
Success = accurate argument analysis, careful reading, and strategic pacing.
Master CR fundamentals: premise, conclusion, assumption, common fallacies.
Master RC: read for structure, answer from the text, avoid outside knowledge.
Practice with official materials and real passages. Consistency beats intensity.

example.label: Your Target
example.text: Score goal: V40–45 (75th+ percentile). Strategy: 80% accuracy, solid argument intuition, confident comprehension.

slides.tip: Verbal skill improves slowly but steadily. Invest 6–8 weeks of consistent practice for a 10-point gain.
slides.warn: There is no shortcut to Verbal mastery—only active reading, argument dissection, and deliberate error review.

gmat-di.title: GMAT Data Insights — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
gmat-di.summary: Master GMAT Focus Data Insights: Data Sufficiency, Multi-Source Reasoning, Table Analysis, Graphics Interpretation, and Two-Part Analysis with data interpretation and logical analysis.

slides.title: Data Insights Section Overview (GMAT Focus Edition)
points: 20 questions in 45 minutes (~2 min 15 sec per question)
Five question types: Data Sufficiency (DS), Multi-Source Reasoning (MSR), Table Analysis (TA), Graphics Interpretation (GI), Two-Part Analysis (TPA)
Integrated reasoning section—combines math, logic, and data analysis
Section-level adaptive: first 5 Qs set difficulty band for remaining 15
Calculator allowed (on-screen tool). Can bookmark up to 3 questions.

example.label: Composition
example.text: Typical: 3–4 DS + 2–3 MSR (one set of sources) + 2–3 TA + 2–3 GI + 2–3 TPA = 20 total.

slides.tip: Unlike Quant, all DI questions count equally toward your 60–90 DI score. One wrong = one point lost.
slides.warn: There is NO partial credit. Each question is binary: correct or incorrect. All or nothing.

slides.title: Data Insights Timing & Pacing Strategy
points: DS questions: ~1:30–2:00 (short, quick logic)
MSR questions: ~3:00–4:00 (read sources, answer 3–4 Qs per set)
TA questions: ~2:30–3:00 (scan table, apply conditions)
GI questions: ~2:00–2:30 (read graph, extract data)
TPA questions: ~2:00–2:30 (understand relationship, solve both parts)
slides.tip: If a question feels like it will take 3+ min, bookmark and move on. Return if time allows.
slides.warn: Don't get stuck on one MSR source set—it contains 3–4 Qs. If one Q is hard, answer the other easy ones first.

slides.title: Data Sufficiency: Concept & Approach
points: Question format: 'Is statement 1 sufficient? Is statement 2 sufficient? Is both together sufficient?'
Answer choices (always the same 5): A (1 only), B (2 only), C (both), D (each alone), E (neither)
Sufficiency = can you determine a unique answer? (Yes/No counts as 'sufficient.')
Do NOT solve the problem. Only assess whether you COULD solve it with the given info.
Test both statements independently first, then together if neither alone was sufficient

example.label: Sufficiency, Not Solution
example.text: Q: 'Is x > 0?' S1: 'x² = 4.' (Sufficient: x = 2 or x = −2, so you know x could be negative or positive—answer is No.) S2: 'x × 3 = 12.' (Sufficient: x = 4, answer is Yes.)

slides.tip: Abbreviate: S1/S2 sufficient (✓) or insufficient (✗). After testing both, pick your answer from the 5 choices.
slides.warn: Sufficiency ≠ uniqueness. You don't need ONE answer; you need to know the answer EXISTS (even if it's no).

slides.title: Data Sufficiency: Testing Method & Common Mistakes
points: Test statement 1 alone: assume it's true, ignore statement 2. Can you answer the question?
Test statement 2 alone: assume it's true, ignore statement 1. Can you answer the question?
If either alone is sufficient, write 'D' (each alone sufficient) or 'A'/'B' (one is sufficient).
If neither alone works, test both together. If together is sufficient, answer 'C.' If not, answer 'E.'
Trap: assuming information from the question text. Only use the statements.

example.label: Testing Order
example.text: Q: 'What is the value of x?' S1: 'x + 5 = 10.' (✓ sufficient: x = 5.) S2: 'x² = 25.' (✗ insufficient: x = 5 or x = −5.) Answer: A (statement 1 only).

slides.tip: Write out 'S1 sufficient?' and 'S2 sufficient?' side by side. Avoid re-reading the question.
slides.warn: If you're not sure, guess A, B, C, or D (avoid E unless you're confident both statements are useless).

slides.title: Data Sufficiency: Algebraic Sufficiency Tricks
points: One equation, one unknown = usually sufficient (e.g., 2x + 3 = 7 → x = 2).
One equation, two unknowns = usually insufficient (e.g., x + y = 10 has infinite solutions).
Two equations, two unknowns = usually sufficient (if independent).
Watch out: sometimes one statement can be derived from another (not independent).
Inequalities: x > 5 tells you x is bounded below, but 'what is x?' is still unanswered (insufficient).

example.label: Trick
example.text: S1: x + y = 10. S2: 2x + 2y = 20. Together: S2 is just 2 × S1 (same line). NOT sufficient. Answer: E.

slides.tip: For two equations, check if one is a multiple of the other (dependent) or truly independent.
slides.warn: Be careful: two equations can look different but be equivalent. Simplify before deciding.

slides.title: Multi-Source Reasoning: Reading & Logic
points: Format: 3–4 information sources (tabs, passages, tables) + 3–4 related questions
Questions may ask: 'Which statement is true?' 'What can be inferred?' 'Is the claim supported?'
Answer types: True/False, Yes/No, For each statement pick Yes/No (3 binary answers)
Strategy: understand the sources first, then answer Qs that reference specific sources
Don't assume info from outside sources. Base answers ONLY on the given data.

example.label: MSR Format
example.text: Tab 1: Company financials 2022–2024. Tab 2: Market report. Tab 3: CEO statement. Q: 'Is the CEO's claim about market share supported by Tab 2?' Answer: Yes/No based on Tab 2 data.

slides.tip: Read the question first to know which source(s) to focus on. Skim the others quickly.
slides.warn: Common trap: mixing data from different years or companies. Note the context of each source.

slides.title: Multi-Source Reasoning: True/False & Inference
points: True statement: directly stated or logically derived from the sources
False statement: contradicts the sources or is unsupported
Inference: conclusion that follows logically from the data, even if not explicitly stated
Do NOT bring outside knowledge. Answer based solely on what's given.
For 'most likely' or 'can be inferred' questions, the answer should feel almost certain from the sources

example.label: Inference
example.text: Source: 'Revenue increased 15% YoY. Operating costs increased 5% YoY.' Inference: 'Profit margin improved.' (True: more revenue, less cost growth = higher margin.)

slides.tip: Reread the source if an answer surprises you. GMAT rarely tricks; re-reading often clarifies.
slides.warn: Avoid extreme inferences ('definitely,' 'impossible'). Stick to what the data directly supports.

slides.title: Table Analysis: Sorting & Filtering
points: Format: a large data table with sortable columns (click to sort A–Z or Z–A)
Questions: 'How many rows meet X criteria?' 'What's the sum of Y where Z > 100?'
Strategy: read the question, identify the column(s) needed, sort if helpful, extract data
Answers: usually numbers (counts, sums, averages) or Yes/No (statement true/false)
Sorting is often the key: sort by relevant column to group data visually

example.label: TA Strategy
example.text: Q: 'How many products have sales > $1M and profit margin > 20%?' 1. Sort by Sales (Z–A) to see high sales. 2. Scan Margin column. 3. Count rows meeting both criteria.

slides.tip: Sketch the calculation before clicking sort. Know what you're looking for.
slides.warn: Sorting changes the order but doesn't change the data. Always verify totals are unchanged after sorting.

slides.title: Table Analysis: Aggregation & Calculation
points: Common questions: sum, average, count, percentage, ratio
Sum: total all values in a column or subset
Average: sum / count
Percentage: (part / whole) × 100 or part / whole as decimal
Ratio: A : B (simplify if needed)
Always double-check arithmetic, especially with large numbers

example.label: Calculation
example.text: Table: Q1 sales $10M, Q2 $12M, Q3 $15M, Q4 $13M. Q: 'What % of annual sales occurred in Q3?' Answer: 15 / (10+12+15+13) = 15/50 = 30%.

slides.tip: Use the calculator for verification, not as a crutch. Know the formula first.
slides.warn: Be careful with units: $M vs $K vs %. Mismatched units cause wrong answers.

slides.title: Graphics Interpretation: Reading Charts & Graphs
points: Formats: bar charts, line graphs, pie charts, scatter plots, histograms
Key elements: title, axes labels, units, legend, data points
Questions: 'What was the value in 2020?' 'Which year had the highest X?' 'What's the trend?'
Answer format: usually fill-in-the-blank (number) or dropdown (select from options)
Strategy: identify the axis (x/y), find the data point, read the value

example.label: GI Read
example.text: Bar chart: Y-axis = Revenue ($M), X-axis = Year (2020–2024). Q: 'Revenue in 2022?' Find 2022 bar height, read Y-value (e.g., $50M).

slides.tip: Check axis labels and units FIRST. A '$M' label means multiply by 1,000,000.
slides.warn: Don't eyeball. Use gridlines or the value label on the graph. Estimating leads to errors.

slides.title: Graphics Interpretation: Trends & Comparisons
points: Trend questions: is the trend increasing, decreasing, or flat? At what rate?
Comparison: which category/year has the highest/lowest value? What's the difference?
Slope/rate: rise / run. Steep slope = fast change; flat = little change
Outliers: look for unusual spikes or dips. They're often tested.
Correlation: two variables move together (positive) or opposite directions (negative)

example.label: Trend
example.text: Line graph: 2020 Revenue $40M, 2021 $50M, 2022 $55M, 2023 $56M. Trend: increasing but slowing (gap shrinking). Rate: +$10M (2020–2021), +$5M (2021–2022), +$1M (2022–2023).

slides.tip: Note rate changes. 'Accelerating' vs 'decelerating' trends are common questions.
slides.warn: Correlation ≠ causation. Two variables moving together doesn't mean one caused the other.

slides.title: Two-Part Analysis: Relationship & Constraints
points: Format: two related questions (Part A and Part B) sharing context
Part A: identify one value/variable. Part B: identify another value/variable.
Constraint: Part B often depends on Part A's answer (or they're independent)
Answers: usually numbers (calculated) or selections from a list
Strategy: solve Part A, use it to constrain Part B, verify both answers are logical

example.label: TPA Structure
example.text: Context: profit = revenue − cost. Part A: 'If revenue = $100M and cost = $30M, profit = ___.' Answer: $70M. Part B: 'If profit must be $50M, cost = ___.' Answer: $50M (using Part A logic or independently).

slides.tip: The two parts are often related but sometimes independent. Read the context carefully.
slides.warn: Do not assume Part B uses Part A's answer unless the context explicitly links them.

slides.title: Two-Part Analysis: Optimization & Trade-offs
points: Optimization: find the best value under constraints (maximize profit, minimize cost)
Trade-off: choose between conflicting goals (high quality vs low cost)
Constraints: limits on variables (budget, time, resources)
Sensitivity: how much can one variable change before the answer shifts?
Both parts must satisfy the overall objective stated in the context

example.label: Trade-off
example.text: Context: Allocate $100 budget between marketing (returns $2 per $1 spent) and R&D (returns $3 per $1 spent). Part A: 'Maximize ROI. Allocate to marketing: ___.' Answer: $0 (R&D has higher return). Part B: 'Allocate to marketing if minimum $10M marketing expense required: ___.' Answer: $10M.

slides.tip: Optimization questions test your ability to compare options. Set up a comparison table.
slides.warn: Always check constraints. A 'best' answer that violates a constraint is wrong.

slides.title: Data Insights Test Strategy: Question Selection
points: Not all question types are equally hard. DSs and GIs tend to be faster.
MSR sets often have 1–2 easy Qs and 1–2 harder Qs. Do the easy ones first.
If a DI question feels like 3+ min, bookmark and move on. Guess strategically.
All questions worth 1 point. Prioritize accuracy over completeness.
Aim for 13–15 correct out of 20 for a strong score (V60–70 range).

example.label: Priority Order
example.text: 1. Do all easy DS Qs (1:30 each). 2. Do GI Qs (2:00 each). 3. TA Qs (2:30 each). 4. MSR easy Qs per set. 5. Return to tough Qs / guess if time runs out.

slides.tip: Bookmark freely. DI is time-pressured; strategic guessing is expected.
slides.warn: Avoid getting trapped in one hard MSR set. Answer the other Qs in the set, then revisit.

slides.title: Common Traps in Data Insights
points: Misreading axes or units (interpreting 'millions' as 'thousands')
Assuming data when it's not provided. Only use the sources given.
Arithmetic errors: miscalculating percentages or ratios under time pressure
Over-interpreting: inferring causation from correlation or trends
Ignoring constraints in TPA: finding an optimal answer that violates a requirement

example.label: Trap
example.text: Graph Y-axis labeled '$M' (millions). You read $50 as 'fifty dollars' instead of '50 million dollars.' Off by 1,000,000x.

slides.tip: After entering an answer, pause and verify units/scale. One second of checking saves wrong answers.
slides.warn: Pressure makes careless errors. Double-check all arithmetic and unit conversions.

slides.title: Integrating Data & Logic: Hybrid Thinking
points: DI questions blend math (calculation) with reasoning (logic and inference)
Don't over-rely on calculator. First understand what the question is asking logically.
Estimate before calculating. Ballpark answers often reveal arithmetic errors.
Use verbal reasoning: 'revenue increased 20%, costs increased 5%, so profit margins improved' (logic first).
Then verify with math. Combining both saves time and catches errors.

example.label: Hybrid
example.text: Q: 'Profit margin for 2023?' Step 1 (Logic): 'Margin = (Revenue − Cost) / Revenue. Higher revenue and controlled cost growth = higher margin.' Step 2 (Math): Calculate exactly.

slides.tip: Talk through the logic before calculating. This clarifies what you're solving.
slides.warn: Purely mathematical solving without understanding the question leads to wrong interpretations.

slides.title: Advanced: Multi-Step MSR Logic Chains
points: Some MSR questions form a chain: Q1's answer informs Q2, which informs Q3
If you get Q1 wrong, Q2's 'correct' answer may hinge on your wrong Q1 answer
Strategy: verify Q1's answer before moving to Q2. Don't cascade errors.
Alternative: answer all Qs independently using the source data (ignore other Qs)
This approach takes more time but avoids cascading errors

example.label: Chain
example.text: Q1: 'Total revenue 2020–2024?' A1: $250M. Q2: 'Average revenue?' Expected: $250M / 5 = $50M. But if your Q1 answer was wrong, Q2 will be wrong too.

slides.tip: For chained Qs, solve independently if unsure about Q1. Sacrifice speed for accuracy.
slides.warn: If a Q1 answer seems obviously wrong, recalculate before proceeding to Q2.

slides.title: Data Insights Practice: Build Speed & Accuracy
points: Start untimed: master accuracy on all DI question types (aim 90%+)
Then introduce time: aim for 2–3 min per Q, achieving 75–80% accuracy
Full-section mocks: 20 Qs in 45 min, simulating real conditions
Log errors: careless math, misreading, overcomplicated logic
Review explanations. DI explanations often reveal faster solution paths.

example.label: Practice Plan
example.text: Week 1: 30 untimed DI Qs (10 DS, 10 TA/GI, 10 TPA). Week 2: same, timed (45 min, 85%+). Week 3: full-section mocks.

slides.tip: Speed comes naturally from repeated practice. Forcing speed first leads to errors.
slides.warn: Do NOT skip to timed practice too early. Build accuracy first; speed follows.

slides.title: Data Sufficiency Deep Dive: Tricky Cases
points: Negative results: 'Is x > 5?' Statement: 'x = 3.' Answer: Yes, sufficient (it's definitively NOT greater than 5).
Range vs unique: 'What is x?' Statement: 'x ∈ [1, 5].' Insufficient (multiple possible values).
Hidden assumptions: 'Is the car fast?' needs a definition of 'fast.' Without it, insufficient.
Variables in statements: sometimes a statement introduces new variables (e.g., 'y = 2x'). Can you still answer the original question?
Real GMAT twists: rarely tested in basic form. Expect subtle traps.

example.label: Negative Result
example.text: Q: 'Is x an even number?' S1: 'x = 5.' (✓ sufficient: it's odd, not even. Sufficient because the answer is definitively No.)

slides.tip: Yes/No questions are sufficient if you can answer definitively, even if the answer is No.
slides.warn: Ranges and inequalities are tricky. 'x > 5' is insufficient for 'what is x?' but sufficient for 'is x > 3?' (yes, always).

slides.title: Final Checklist: Data Insights Mastery
points: Data Sufficiency: test S1, test S2, test both. Know the 5 answer choices cold.
MSR: read sources, answer Qs based ONLY on given data.
Table Analysis: sort as needed, calculate sums/averages/percentages, verify units.
Graphics Interpretation: read axes and units, locate data points, avoid eyeballing.
TPA: solve Part A, use it (if dependent) to constrain Part B. Verify both satisfy context.

example.label: Your Score Target
example.text: DI goal: 60–70 (75th+ percentile). Strategy: 75–80% accuracy, strategic bookmarking, fast fundamentals.

slides.tip: DI is the lowest-scored section on average. A 60+ is competitive. Aim for 13–15 correct out of 20.

example.text: Mon: 5 DS (timed). Tue: 1 MSR set + 2 TA (timed). Wed: 3 GI + 2 TPA (timed). Thu: full-section mock. Review errors daily.

slides.tip: DI improves fastest with volume practice. 50+ full-section Qs will reveal patterns and edge cases.
slides.warn: Do NOT memorize answers to practice Qs. Each question type has variations; focus on method.

slides.title: Closing: Your Data Insights Win
points: GMAT Focus Data Insights is 20 questions (mix of 5 types), 45 minutes, calculator allowed.
Success = careful data reading, logical inference, and strategic time management.
